name: Českolipský buk lesní

location.address: Small public park (parčík) at the corner of Moskevská and U Kartounky streets, near the city hospital, Česká Lípa

No access restriction found; a public park beside a hospital reads as ordinary open ground.
story:
The state protects a circle twelve metres wide around this copper beech, and the circle sits on a street corner beside a hospital. Its trunk measures 3.85 metres round, a serious waistline for a tree in a patch of town green rather than a castle park.

It is not an ordinary beech. The Czech nature conservation agency, AOPK, records it as the purple form, the copper beech, whose leaves open a deep purple in spring and darken through the summer. The agency added it to the national list of memorial trees on 15 October 2010 under a plain working name, Buk lesní v Moskevské ulici, the beech on Moskevská street. Locally it goes by something prouder: Českolipský buk lesní, the beech of Česká Lípa.

The park it stands in is barely a park at all, a small square of grass at the corner of Moskevská and U Kartounky, with the hospital next door. Nothing else in it competes for attention.

Two things we do not know, and would like to. Nobody has published an age for it, so we will not invent one; if you know when it was planted, tell us. And the most recent dated photograph we could find was taken in 2012. The register still lists the tree as protected and records no loss, which is good news but not the same as somebody having seen it this year. If you walk past, let us know it is standing.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its purple leaves in the growing season and a trunk 3.85 metres round. It stands in the small park at the corner of Moskevská and U Kartounky, beside the city hospital.

story:
A beech 4.10 metres round stands in open country outside Mokřice, a hamlet belonging to the small town of Krásná Hora nad Vltavou, and according to OpenStreetMap somebody has put a picnic table right beside it.

The Czech nature conservation agency, AOPK, lists it as a memorial tree under the simplest name possible, Buk v Mokřicích, the beech at Mokřice. That entry is the whole of its paperwork. We found no plaque story, no founding legend and no local history page, which is unusual for a Czech tree that made the national list. What the register does keep is the girth, and 4.10 metres is a lot of beech for a tree standing out in the fields of the Příbram district rather than in a castle park or an old forest.

So this one arrives without a story attached and has to be judged on its trunk alone, which is a test it passes.

We have to be straight about two gaps. Nobody has published its age, and we would rather leave the field empty than guess. And we found no dated photograph of it at all, only the register entry and two pictures of unknown date, so we cannot say when anyone last reported it standing. The register itself records no loss. If you walk out to Mokřice, tell us what you find, and bring a tape measure if you fancy checking the state's number.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 4.10 metres round, a big beech out in open country. It stands near the hamlet of Mokřice, at the spot where OpenStreetMap marks a picnic table.

best_time.label: October, when the beech turns copper and gold

name: Baobá de Nísia Floresta

location.address: Central plaza in front of the church, Centro, Nísia Floresta
location.neighbourhood: Centro, Nísia Floresta, Rio Grande do Norte

access: Free. Stands in the town's central plaza, in front of the church, near the bus terminal and old railway station; open public ground.
transport: Central Nísia Floresta, walking distance of the town centre; the town itself sits roughly 45 minutes by road from Natal (day-trip range, but by car/bus rather than a city walk)
verify_notes: DELIVERED under the register-alone rule as an official designation rather than a national government register: the municipality's own page states the baobab is protected by Federal Law 4.771/65 and Municipal Law 169/70, with two further municipal laws in 2007 (Lei Complementar 001/2007 designating the surrounding area 'of scenic interest', Lei Complementar 003/2007 declaring the baobab itself Environmental Heritage of the Municipality). Per a plaque by the tree (quoted on the municipality's own page), it was planted in 1877 by a citizen named Manoel Júnior, giving a documented planting date (about 149 years as of 2026; stated broadly as 'about 150 years'). A widely repeated local legend says it was brought/planted by an enslaved African person carrying seeds from their homeland, and a separate disputed claim ties it to Saint-Exupery's Little Prince (he supposedly saw it on a transatlantic flight in the 1920s-30s); NEITHER legend is stated as fact, only as local claims, and they appear to be in tension with the plaque's own 1877/Manoel Júnior planting story, which the writer should note as a genuine disagreement between sources rather than resolve. FLAGGED for that disagreement and because the exact 1877 date rests on a plaque and the municipality's own retelling rather than an independent document. OSM tags this tree individually (natural=tree, name 'Baobá de Nísia') at the coordinate used here, on Rua João Batista Gondim, matching the 'central plaza near the church' description exactly. No girth or height found in the time available. Not checked with lifecheck.py (outside Europe; script may not have imagery coverage there, not attempted this pass).
story:
Nísia Floresta will tell you that Antoine de Saint-Exupéry saw this baobab from the air on one of his flights across the Atlantic, and that it ended up in The Little Prince, the book whose tiny planet is overrun by baobabs. The plaque standing beside the tree tells a plainer story: it was planted in 1877 by a local man named Manoel Júnior.

Those two accounts do not sit easily together, and there is a third. A widely repeated tradition holds that the tree grew from seeds an enslaved African carried from home. The plaque, quoted on the municipality's own page, is the only one of the three with a name and a year attached, which makes the tree about 150 years old: young, for a species that can live for well over a thousand. The other stories cannot be proven, and nobody has ruled them out either.

What is not in doubt is how seriously the town takes it. The baobab has been protected under Brazil's 1965 forest code and a municipal law of 1970, and in 2007 the council went further twice over: one law declared the ground around it of scenic interest, a second named the tree itself Environmental Heritage of the Municipality.

It stands in the central plaza in front of the church, a short walk from the bus terminal and the old railway station, on open public ground. Nobody has published its girth. If you visit with a tape measure, we would like to know.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the baobab in the central plaza, with a plaque beside it recording its 1877 planting. It stands in front of the church, near the bus terminal and the old railway station.

name: Árvore do Amor
age_estimate: locally said to be over 300 years

location.address: Barra de Maxaranguape beach, Av. Cabo de São Roque, Maxaranguape, Rio Grande do Norte

access: Free. A well-known public tourist spot on Barra de Maxaranguape beach; OpenStreetMap tags it tourism=yes by name. No gate or ticket found in any source.
transport: Maxaranguape municipality, roughly 55km up the coast from Natal; a day trip by car or bus, not a walk or short hop from the city itself
verify_notes: CORRECTS the original lead, filed under the name 'Árvore dos Amores, Natal-RN' from a Commons photo filename. It is NOT in Natal: every news source (Terra, Tribuna do Norte, Band, the Maxaranguape municipal government's own site) places it at Barra de Maxaranguape beach, Maxaranguape municipality, about 55km up the coast from Natal, and it should be its own place rather than presented as in-town Natal (day-trip boundary rule). It is two 'gameleira' (a Brazilian common name covering several native Ficus species) trees whose trunks and canopies have grown together, forming a heart shape when the shadow falls a certain way at mid-morning; treated as one collectible ensemble point since there is one obvious place to stand. Age is a widely repeated local figure, 'mais de 300 anos' / 'over 300 years old', appearing consistently across multiple independent news outlets but with no cited source, measurement or documented planting date behind it; kept exactly as vague as the sources give it, per the estimate-vs-invention rule, and flagged as a local claim rather than a measured fact. On 2024-02-27 someone deliberately cut through several of its exposed roots (a criminal act reported to police and environmental agencies Idema/Ibama); as of the article's reporting the tree had survived and officials said the cuts were unlikely to kill it though could invite disease, so this is recorded as an act of vandalism the tree survived, not evidence of decline. Coordinate is an OSM node tagged 'Árvore do Amor'/tourism=yes; a second natural=tree node sits about 13m away, likely marking the second joined trunk. No girth found. Not checked with lifecheck.py (outside Europe; script may not have imagery coverage there, not attempted this pass).
story:
At the right hour of the morning this tree throws a shadow shaped like a heart, which is how a fig on a beach north of Natal became the Árvore do Amor, the Tree of Love.

Strictly, it is two trees. Both are gameleiras, the name Brazilians give to several native figs, and over the years their trunks and crowns have grown into one another until they read as a single tree with one obvious place to stand. The shadow does the rest, but only when the sun sits at the right angle in the middle of the morning. Come at noon and you get a large, ordinary patch of shade.

Everyone locally will tell you it is more than 300 years old. Every news report repeats the figure and none of them says where it comes from, so treat it as the beach's own tradition rather than a measurement.

In February 2024 somebody took a blade to it. Several of the exposed roots were cut through deliberately, and the case went to the police and to the state and federal environmental agencies. The tree survived. Officials said the cuts were unlikely to kill it, although open wounds can let disease in, so a report from anyone who has seen it lately is welcome.

It stands on Barra de Maxaranguape beach, about 55 kilometres up the coast from Natal: a day out by car or bus, free, with no gate and no ticket. Nobody has published its girth.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by two fig trunks grown together into one crown, whose shadow falls as a heart in mid-morning. It stands on Barra de Maxaranguape beach, where it is the best-known sight.

name: Figueira das Lágrimas

location.address: Estrada das Lágrimas (near no. 515), Sacomã, São Paulo

access: Free. Stands in Praça Figueira das Lágrimas, a small square the Ipiranga sub-prefecture created around it in 2020 specifically to preserve and open the site to the public.
transport: Sacomã district, southern São Paulo; nearest metro/bus stop not established this pass
story:
São Paulo named this tree after the crying. The Figueira das Lágrimas, the Fig Tree of Tears, stands on the Estrada das Lágrimas in the south of the city, and this is where Paulistanos said goodbye to people leaving for the coast or for other parts of Brazil.

The farewells gave it its name and most of its history. Mothers parted here from sons sent to the Paraguayan War in the 1860s. Law students from the faculty at Largo São Francisco walked out to the fig to see off friends heading home. Documents place it as an already mature tree in 1862, and botanists estimate its age at more than 250 years, which is why it is often called the oldest tree in São Paulo.

A more recent story claims it for Brazilian independence, saying Dom Pedro I passed under it on the way to his famous cry by the Ipiranga in 1822. It spread around the 2022 bicentennial. It may be true; it is also exactly the kind of story a famous old tree attracts, so take it lightly.

The city has taken the tree seriously. CONPRESP, São Paulo's heritage council, listed it as a protected landmark in 2016, and in 2020 the Ipiranga sub-prefecture built a small public square around it. In 2022 a sapling grown from it was planted between Avenida Dom Pedro I and the Praça do Monumento.

We know it is a fig but not which species. If you can tell, let us know.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the old fig at the heart of Praça Figueira das Lágrimas, the small square built around it in 2020 on Estrada das Lágrimas. Our pin marks the road nearby, so look for the square.

name: Cipreste Farroupilha

location.neighbourhood: Centro, Guaíba, Rio Grande do Sul

access: Free. Stands in Praça Gomes Jardim, a public square in central Guaíba; open ground.
transport: Central Guaíba, a short ferry/road trip across the Rio Guaíba from Porto Alegre; nearest stop not established this pass
verify_notes: An official civic symbol rather than a register entry: the tree appears in Guaíba's own municipal anthem, coat of arms and flag, which is about as strong a local-government designation as exists without a formal heritage register, corroborated by its own Wikipedia article and local news/tourism sources (guaiba.online, a TV Guaíba Online column; wikimapia's community-mapped location). History: local tradition holds it was planted around 1680 to mark the grave of a Spanish army commander killed while passing through hunting cattle, a custom of the era; and that on 1835-09-19 Farroupilha Revolution leaders (Bento Gonçalves da Silva, Onofre Pires, Gomes Jardim) planned their invasion of Porto Alegre in its shade, giving the tree and the revolution its name. Age is a local estimate, 'mais de 300 anos' ('more than 300 years'), consistent with the ~1680 planting tradition (about 346 years as of 2026) but resting on oral history/folklore rather than a document, so kept as a broad range rather than a precise figure. Location is the plaza (Praça Gomes Jardim) rather than a tree-level pin, so location_precision is approximate. Species is 'cipreste' (cypress); no source found specifying which Cupressus species, so left genus-only. No girth found. Not checked with lifecheck.py (outside Europe; script may not have imagery coverage there, not attempted this pass).
story:
This cypress is on the flag of the city it grows in, on the city's coat of arms, and in its anthem. Guaíba has its reasons. On 19 September 1835, by the town's own account, Bento Gonçalves da Silva, Onofre Pires and Gomes Jardim sat in its shade and planned the attack on Porto Alegre that opened the Farroupilha Revolution, the ten-year war in which Rio Grande do Sul tried to break away from the Brazilian Empire. The tree took the revolution's name, and the square around it is named after Gomes Jardim.

The story of how it got here is older and stranger. Local tradition holds that it was planted around 1680 over the grave of a Spanish army commander, killed while passing through on a cattle hunt, at a time when marking a grave with a tree was the custom. That would put it at something over 300 years, which is the figure Guaíba gives, but the date rests on oral history rather than any document, so read it as the town's memory rather than a measurement.

Nobody has recorded which cypress species it is, or how thick it is, and our pin puts you in the square rather than at the trunk. If you know either, or can stand at it and tell us where it is, we would like to hear.

Guaíba sits across the water from Porto Alegre, a short trip by ferry or road. The square is public and free.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the old cypress of Praça Gomes Jardim, the tree Guaíba puts on its flag and coat of arms. The pin marks the square rather than the trunk, so look for the cypress in it.
